prize_parts.citation: for their theoretical analysis of how special-interest politics shape trade policy

statement.case_for: Grossman and Helpman turned trade protection from an exogenous policy wedge into an equilibrium outcome of lobbying and electoral incentives. The Protection for Sale framework is a clean, portable model that gave trade-policy politics a testable structure. It has been taught, extended and used in empirical work on tariff structures and trade agreements for three decades, and it belongs to the broader formal political-economy tradition. Their wider joint programme on innovation, growth and technology diffusion across open economies reinforces the case, though the citation I propose stays within the shortlisted discovery. Attribution is unusually clean, since this is a stable two-person partnership with jointly authored core papers and books. Maturity is not a concern. The trade-theory ground covered by the 2008 prize (new trade theory and trade patterns) is distinct from this contribution, which concerns the politics of policy formation.
statement.case_against: The empirical record for the specific Protection for Sale predictions is mixed. The influence is largely conceptual and methodological rather than a settled empirical finding. Part of the trade-theory space was recognised in 2008. Helpman is also credited on B041, so a committee that prefers a firm-heterogeneity prize would compete for the same laureate. This entry's narrow description may understate or misframe the Grossman-Helpman programme, and the committee could reasonably prefer a candidate with broader recent empirical or policy reach.

responses.point: Hassler ranks the Melitz-Helpman firm-heterogeneity candidate (B041) first. He argues that selection into exporting and reallocation introduced a new channel for the gains from trade and reshaped both theory and empirics, and that it builds on the 2008 prize.
responses.response: I agree that Melitz (2003) is a major contribution and that the evidence base is broad. But Hassler's own caveat that heterogeneous-firm ideas have precursors (Bernard-Jensen empirics, Hopenhayn-style selection) shows the attribution is looser than for Grossman-Helpman. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum are not credited on B041, which makes the laureate set contestable. I also read B041 as the more direct successor to the new trade theory recognised in 2008. B013 opens a different question, namely why policy takes the form it does. If the committee prefers the trade-theory route, I would accept B041 as a serious alternative but not as a replacement for B013 on scientific grounds.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B038 (Autor, Hanson, Dorn) first and B013 only sixth. She values the combination of new data with an explanatory framework and notes that the empirical support for protection-for-sale predictions has been mixed.
responses.response: The empirical point is fair, and it is my main reservation about B013. Mixed tests of one specific functional form do not undo the framework's role in organising later empirical work on tariff structure and trade agreements. A prize rewards the idea and its consequences, not only the survival of every prediction. I also accept her case for B038 on the China-shock evidence. She and most other members propose Dorn, not Katz, as the third name, and that persuades me. Katz's contribution on the education-technology race is better placed on B002 or a separate wage-structure claim. I have moved toward Autor, Hanson and Dorn as the more defensible grouping if B038 advances, though overlap with the 2024 prize on technology and the debate over China-shock magnitudes still give me pause.

responses.point: Boppart ranks Kiyotaki-Moore (B012) first. He argues that its collateral-constraint amplification mechanism is foundational for macro-finance, is validated by 2008, and is best credited to the clean two-person core, with the 2022 prize overlap as the main risk.
responses.response: I largely agree on the science and attribution, and I proposed the same two names in my own opening. Credit Cycles is a rigorous mechanism with decades of confirmation. I place it just behind B013 because of the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises, which covered neighbouring ground. Boppart's own uncertainty about including Gertler and Gilchrist is real. Teorell adds Gertler, but that blurs a clean attribution and overlaps with the Bernanke line. I would keep B012 as a two-person alternative and would not enlarge it.

responses.point: Enflo ranks Persson-Tabellini (B027) second. She argues that they created the modern formal and empirical study of how constitutions and electoral rules shape fiscal policy, that the work is very mature, and that the main risks are the recent institutions prize and whether Besley is included.
responses.response: I share her view of the field-defining character of this body of work, which is why I ranked B027 second. The strongest argument for B027 is attribution and maturity. Her point that Persson and Tabellini form the clean core, with Besley a judgement call, matches my own uncertainty. My reservation is the proximity to the 2024 prize. B027 is also the candidate that has been least examined by colleagues, since only two of us ranked it. I therefore keep it as an alternative rather than the lead. Its political-economy logic is also close to B013, so a committee that wants this area recognised could weigh the two against each other on merit, not on counts.

uncertainties: Whether the committee judges the 2008 trade prize to have already covered enough of trade theory to make a Grossman-Helpman award look redundant.
How much weight the committee gives to the mixed empirical support for Protection for Sale predictions against the framework's conceptual influence.
Whether Helpman is better credited for B013 or for B041, and whether a combined trade configuration would be coherent given the single-laureate overlap.
Whether B038 (with Dorn instead of Katz) has stronger scientific and policy reach than B013, and how the 2024 technology-and-institutions prize affects that comparison.
Whether Besley should join Persson and Tabellini on B027, and whether the 2024 institutions prize makes that area too close.
statement.conflict_note: Giovanni Violante, a long-term co-author per my profile, is credited on B004. That framework also builds on my own earlier heterogeneous-agent work with Anthony Smith, so I am not proposing B004 and give it no weight in this stage. The profile also lists co-authorship with John Hassler (chair) and Timo Boppart (co-opted member), and I have weighed their arguments on scientific merit. No connection to Helpman, Grossman, Persson, Tabellini, Kiyotaki or Moore is apparent from the supplied profile.
